title: The Omnicorp charter
summary: A design question: what could an organisation become if AI were part of its foundations, and continual development were its purpose?

sections.heading: The question we are exploring
paragraphs: Omnicorp begins with a question about organisation. If AI can contribute directly to research, judgment and execution, how should a company be designed around that possibility? Adding an assistant to an existing process is one answer. Reconsidering the process, its responsibilities and its feedback is a more demanding one.

The ambition is broad, but its cornerstone is specific: continually improve the organisation’s ability to understand, learn and act. Products and work in the world give that development resources, constraints and consequences. They help reveal whether a new capability is useful beyond the environment in which it was created.

sections.heading: The organisation is part of the invention
paragraphs: The charter uses electrification as a historical analogy. A new source of power did not automatically produce a better factory. Layout, machinery, workflow and skills had to change together. The analogy suggests that the productive use of AI will also require complementary changes in how work is arranged.

This is a design argument, not a prediction that history will repeat on a particular schedule. A capable model alone does not supply a trustworthy organisation. Clear ownership, usable information, appropriate tools, independent evaluation and human accountability all shape what the technology can accomplish.

sections.heading: A purpose with contact with reality
paragraphs: Continual development does not mean treating every change as progress. A better process should improve a relevant outcome, retain valuable capabilities and remain answerable to its intended purpose. The organisation needs ways to distinguish a useful advance from novelty, a persuasive explanation or a result that only works on familiar examples.

Useful activity provides that contact with reality. Building something people need creates feedback that internal demonstrations cannot supply. The commercial and practical dimensions therefore belong inside the design, while remaining means of sustaining the larger purpose rather than its complete definition.

sections.heading: A blueprint with different confidence levels
paragraphs: The nearer questions concern software, research, coordination and repeatable workflows. These allow relatively short feedback cycles and bounded experiments. The further questions concern physical operations, infrastructure and organisations spanning many domains. Those involve additional constraints and much greater uncertainty.

Omnicorp keeps both horizons in view without treating them as equally established. A design for an agent team is not evidence that the team will work reliably. A path toward a physical industry is not proof of permission, engineering feasibility or operational readiness. Each extension needs evidence appropriate to its consequences.

sections.heading: How to read these notes
paragraphs: These public documents share an evolving body of thinking: the architecture, the growth path, the proposed workforce and the questions behind continual development. They are design notes, not a report that the complete organisation already exists.

The invitation is to examine the structure of the idea. Which parts would make learning cumulative? Which decisions need human judgment? What would show that a proposed system can act more effectively while preserving continuity and trust? Those questions matter more than an impressive diagram.

questions: What would count as useful cumulative development?
Which organisational complements must change together?
Where does the analogy with earlier technologies stop being useful?

title: The organisation as a system
summary: Five connected layers describe how human direction, agents, operating practices and useful work could support cumulative capability.

sections.heading: Design around the work
paragraphs: The blueprint asks how to arrange an organisation when AI can be an actor in its workflows. The starting point is the work itself: what information a task requires, who can make a decision, which tools are appropriate and how a result will be judged. The organisation should make those relationships explicit.

The wider purpose is continual development of understanding and agency. The architecture describes ways to support that purpose through practical activity. Its layers are a map for reasoning about dependencies, not a claim that every component has been implemented or that the design guarantees success.

sections.heading: Human direction and an agent platform
paragraphs: The first layer is the human core. It holds purpose, judgment, trust and accountability. It decides which objectives deserve attention and accepts responsibility for consequential choices. Delegating execution does not make consent, legitimacy or liability disappear.

The second layer is an agent platform: models, tools, coordination, memory and visibility into what happened. Different tasks may need different capabilities. A strong system makes those capabilities available without giving every participant unrestricted access or assuming that a confident response is a reliable one.

sections.heading: Operating practices and useful outcomes
paragraphs: The third layer is the operating system of the organisation. This means shared practices rather than a particular software product: clear task briefs, records of decisions, evaluation methods, ownership rules and escalation paths. These practices are part of what the organisation learns and retains.

The fourth layer consists of product engines: repeatable combinations of people, agents and processes directed at useful outcomes. Research, software and creative work are examples of possible domains. The fifth layer concerns the resources that sustain the system and allow accepted improvements to be carried forward.

sections.heading: Coordination must have a shape
paragraphs: The proposed coordination rule is straightforward: investigation can spread across independent workers, while a coherent decision or shared artifact needs an identifiable owner. Parallel research is valuable when questions can be separated. Concurrent editing becomes costly when participants need to negotiate every change.

Work should arrive with an objective, boundaries and observable success conditions. Evaluation belongs in the architecture from the beginning. A maker and an independent reviewer have different roles; their agreement is useful only when the reviewer can inspect the result and challenge its assumptions.

sections.heading: Learning without losing control
paragraphs: Accepted work can improve the next cycle through better tools, reusable context and clearer practices. That feedback is the beginning of organisational development. Changes to governing instructions or authority deserve explicit review because a system should not quietly redefine what counts as success.

The design also calls for limited permissions, bounded effort and clear human intervention points. More agents do not automatically mean more useful work. The relevant question is whether coordination and evaluation can keep pace with generation. Future changes to model capabilities would extend this question, while preserving human direction and evidence independent of the proposed improvement.

questions: Which layer is currently limiting useful work?
Can a reviewer challenge a result without depending on its maker’s explanation?
How should a system retain learning while keeping authority explicit?

title: From one operator to a larger organisation
summary: A staged model for increasing responsibility and scope only as useful work becomes repeatable and verifiable.

sections.heading: Growth begins with competence
paragraphs: The first stage is an operator learning to direct and judge work in a domain they understand. Access to a model is widely available; the harder skill is deciding what to ask, recognising a good result and identifying what still needs a person. Early progress is therefore competence, not the appearance of a large organisation.

A useful starting loop is to investigate a question, form a plan, execute a bounded task, examine the result independently and retain what was learned. Repetition should make acceptable work easier to produce and easier to recognise. A growing collection of unexamined outputs does not establish that improvement.

sections.heading: One repeatable engine
paragraphs: The next stage focuses on one kind of useful outcome for a specific audience. The process remains close to its human operator, who reviews much of the work and learns where the system succeeds or fails. The aim is a repeatable relationship between a real need, a method and an accepted result.

Distribution and trust belong beside production. The ability to make something does not show that anyone needs it or understands its value. Equally, demand does not excuse weak quality. The organisation needs feedback from the people it serves as well as evidence about how the work was produced.

sections.heading: A small coordinated team
paragraphs: As a process becomes understandable and repeatable, a small team of agents and human specialists may take on more of it. The human role can shift toward allocation, editing and exceptions. That shift should follow demonstrated reliability rather than the desire to remove a person from the loop.

The main danger is a gap between generation and verification. More outputs can make the system look productive while defects accumulate. Independent review, explicit ownership and limits on concurrent work help expose that gap. Evaluation capacity needs to grow with the responsibility being delegated.

sections.heading: Several engines, then wider domains
paragraphs: A larger organisation could reuse its operating practices across several kinds of work. Each new engine would still need its own evidence: a relevant need, a credible delivery process and an appropriate way to judge outcomes. Reuse should reduce setup friction without flattening important differences between domains.

Physical and regulated activities introduce constraints that software demonstrations cannot settle. Expertise, permissions, liability, equipment and elapsed time may all matter. Working alongside experienced operators is one possible route to learning those constraints. It is not equivalent to being ready to own or operate the activity directly.

sections.heading: A ladder, not a timetable
paragraphs: These stages describe changing conditions, not promised dates or a claim that a one-person conglomerate has been demonstrated. The further stages are deliberately more speculative. Movement should depend on whether the organisation can preserve quality, continuity and accountability at the next level of responsibility.

The governing purpose remains cumulative understanding and agency. Scale is useful when it supports that purpose through better work and stronger feedback. A larger agent roster, a wider portfolio or greater output alone cannot establish progress. Sometimes the next advance will be a simpler process that can be understood, evaluated and repeated.

questions: What evidence makes a process ready for delegation?
Can evaluation keep pace with the proposed increase in output?
Which responsibilities change when work enters the physical world?

title: Roles that make collaboration legible
summary: Personas define responsibilities, boundaries and handoffs for a proposed workforce; they are not proof of autonomous capability.

sections.heading: The brief is the role
paragraphs: A persona in the Omnicorp design is an operating contract. Its name makes the role memorable, but the substance is its mandate: the objective, permitted tools, required inputs, expected output and conditions for escalation. A vivid identity cannot compensate for an ambiguous assignment.

The proposed workforce separates responsibilities that benefit from distinct contexts. Research may explore several independent questions. Implementation needs a bounded task and clear ownership. Verification needs room to disagree. The design avoids assuming that a group conversation will automatically turn these different activities into a coherent result.

sections.heading: Atlas, Oracle and Forge
paragraphs: Atlas is the orchestration role. It translates a human objective into a plan, assigns bounded tasks and brings the results together. A useful orchestrator makes assumptions visible and keeps the final decision understandable. It does not gain authority simply because it coordinates other agents.

Oracle represents research and synthesis: examine sources, preserve uncertainty and produce an answer whose claims can be traced. Forge represents software architecture: clarify the intended behaviour, identify boundaries and define work that an implementer can carry out. These roles distinguish investigating a question from deciding how a system should be built.

sections.heading: Smith, Warden and Sentinel
paragraphs: Smith is the implementer, responsible for a defined piece of work. The role needs enough access to complete that task, with a clear point at which difficulty or ambiguity should be escalated. Work ownership limits accidental conflicts and makes the result easier to inspect.

Warden is the independent verifier. It examines the delivered artifact rather than accepting the maker’s narrative, and tries to identify where the result fails its intended conditions. Sentinel adds a security perspective: limited permissions, appropriate isolation and attention to what an agent could access or change. These are proposed responsibilities, not assurances that failures are impossible.

sections.heading: Creative work, distribution and continuity
paragraphs: Muse is the creative direction role, supported by writing, visual and distribution functions. Its purpose is to preserve editorial judgment and originality when producing content becomes easier. Herald represents the relationship between useful work and the people who might need it, with trust and truthful claims part of that responsibility.

Archivist and Compass represent continuity: reusable knowledge, records of decisions and a reliable account of who owns the next action. Financial recordkeeping and analysis have their own bounded roles. The broader principle is to keep consequential authority distinct from the ability to generate an analysis or recommendation.

sections.heading: A team must earn its complexity
paragraphs: Specialisation helps when it creates independent work or protects a valuable separation of concerns. It hurts when every participant needs the same large context or several agents compete to control one artifact. Small teams with explicit handoffs are the starting design; adding members requires a reason.

A future community might also diagnose and improve the capabilities of its members. That remains a conditional research direction. Consensus within the group would not demonstrate an improvement. Candidates would need independent evaluation, retained parent versions and an explicit decision about what to integrate. Human purpose and responsibility remain above the persona roster.

questions: Does each role have an objective and an observable deliverable?
Which tasks benefit from separation, and which need one owner?
Can the team reject an attractive result that does not survive independent review?

title: The capacity to keep developing
summary: The cornerstone of Omnicorp: improve understanding and agency while preserving purpose, continuity and contact with reality.

sections.heading: The purpose behind the engines
paragraphs: Omnicorp’s founding purpose is continual development of the organisation’s ability to understand, learn and act. Useful products and physical activity sustain that development and expose it to consequences outside its own reasoning. They are essential sources of resources and feedback, while the ambition extends beyond producing more output.

The transistor offers an analogy for the scale of possibility: a foundational capability can enable uses its first builders cannot fully picture. That is a way to think about uncertainty and preparation, not evidence that AI follows a particular curve or that a singularity has an arrival date.

sections.heading: Improvement could belong to a community
paragraphs: One conditional possibility is a community whose members help improve one another. Task performers could generate experience, diagnosticians could identify recurring failures, editors could propose changes and independent evaluators could test the candidates. Integration would be a distinct responsibility rather than an automatic response to a positive report.

This differs from imagining a single model that must understand every task and reliably rewrite itself. Progress might concern tools, communication or the allocation of work before it reaches model capabilities. Direct changes to model weights are a further possibility whose usefulness, reliability and cost would need to be established for a named task.

sections.heading: Adaptation is not the same as capability creation
paragraphs: Temporary specialisation could make a general foundation useful in several settings: apply a task-specific change, test it and later restore or switch it. But the ability to edit a model does not establish the ability to find beneficial edits, add missing knowledge or preserve unrelated skills.

Early research on direct weight editing illustrates why that distinction matters. A change may remove an obstruction to an existing capability without creating a new one. Such results can motivate better questions, but they do not demonstrate an indefinitely improving organisation or a reliable community of model editors.

sections.heading: Intelligence and the physical world
paragraphs: Improved understanding could help design better machines and infrastructure, which could support further development. This is a possible feedback loop rather than a guarantee of acceleration. Physical systems still require engineering, maintenance, permissions and resources. Some observations and experiments take time that faster design cannot eliminate.

The same practical approach applies to software. A model might generate interfaces and workflows when needed, while records, reliable execution, communication and access control still require dependable implementations. The useful question is which representation performs a job well, rather than whether every operation can be absorbed into a model.

sections.heading: What would make development credible?
paragraphs: A meaningful evaluation would define a task, retain an unchanged starting point and test proposed improvements on outcomes that were not used to design them. It would compare simpler alternatives, examine regressions and account for the full effort required to adapt and operate the candidate.

Accepted gains should survive repetition and unfamiliar cases. Parent versions, change history and rollback preserve continuity; independent evaluation prevents a candidate from making its own standard easier. These are future design questions, not a report of a running self-improvement system. The objective and the properties that must endure need explicit human direction.

sections.heading: Two turning points, and several kinds of mathematical progress
paragraphs: ChatGPT’s public research preview on 30 November 2022 is our public-encounter milestone. Claude Opus 4.5, released on 24 November 2025, is a developer-work turning point in Omnicorp’s interpretation: delegating substantial work became more compelling to us. That is not a claim that developers first used AI in late 2025; Copilot was already available earlier.

The evidence now includes contest proofs at IMO silver and gold standard, research-level algorithm discovery, a new zeta-function result with external mathematical follow-through, and formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem. These are different achievements. Formalizing a known proof is not discovering a theorem, and the zeta work did not solve the Riemann hypothesis.

The Observatory attaches sources and limits to each milestone. Its curve is schematic: the date of the present is known, but the height of its dot is an editorial choice with no defined accuracy probability. The numerical forecasts instead concern specific new public records, fixed criteria and deadlines.

questions: Does an apparent gain persist on unfamiliar tasks?
What capabilities and commitments must survive each change?
When does the full cost of adaptation outweigh its repeated benefit?
